subject: dbms
title: Unit 2 — Textbook Exercises (Silberschatz Ch3–5, Elmasri/Navathe Ch6–7)

items.q: **(Silberschatz, Practice Ex. 3.1d)** To 'find all instructors earning the highest salary (there may be several tied)', the robust approach is:
items.explain: Comparing each row to the scalar MAX returns every instructor tied for the top salary; ORDER BY ... LIMIT 1 would drop the ties.

items.q: **(Silberschatz, Practice Ex. 3.2)** Grade points for a section = credits × numeric-points-for-grade. Computing a student's GPA (total grade points ÷ total credits) across courses requires:
options: Joining takes with grade_points and course, then SUM of (credits×points) divided by SUM of credits
items.explain: GPA aggregates over the joined takes–course–grade_points rows: SUM(credits×points)/SUM(credits). The exercise also warns to handle NULL grades, which aggregates ignore.

items.q: **(Silberschatz, Practice Ex. 3.5)** To assign a letter grade from a numeric score (F if <40, C if <60, B if <80, else A), the natural SQL construct is:
options: A CASE expression with ordered WHEN conditions
items.explain: CASE WHEN score<40 THEN 'F' WHEN score<60 THEN 'C' ... ELSE 'A' END. Because the first matching WHEN wins, the bounds must be ordered ascending.

items.q: **(Silberschatz, Practice Ex. 3.6)** Since LIKE is case-sensitive in most systems, how do you find departments whose name contains 'sci' regardless of case?
options: Apply lower() to the column: WHERE lower(dept_name) LIKE '%sci%'
items.explain: Normalise case on both sides with lower() (or upper()) so the pattern match is case-insensitive: WHERE lower(dept_name) LIKE '%sci%'.

items.q: **(Silberschatz, Practice Ex. 3.8a)** 'Find each customer who has an account but NOT a loan' is most directly expressed with:
options: Set difference: (customers with an account) EXCEPT (customers with a loan)
items.explain: 'A but not B' is set difference — depositor IDs EXCEPT borrower IDs (or equivalently NOT IN / NOT EXISTS).

items.q: **(Silberschatz, Ex. 3.19)** Which are valid reasons a NULL value might be introduced into a database?
options: The value is unknown, or it is not applicable to that row
items.explain: NULL marks a value that is unknown (not yet known) or inapplicable (does not exist for that entity) — the two canonical reasons given in the text.

items.q: **(Silberschatz, Ex. 3.20)** The exercise asks you to show that, in SQL, `<> ALL` is identical to:
items.explain: value <> ALL (set) is TRUE exactly when value differs from every element — i.e. it is not in the set — so <> ALL ≡ NOT IN. (Dually, = SOME ≡ IN.)

items.q: **(Silberschatz, Ex. 3.21b)** 'Find each member who has borrowed EVERY book published by McGraw-Hill' is a division query, best written with:
options: Double NOT EXISTS (no McGraw-Hill book that the member has not borrowed)
items.explain: 'Borrowed every X' = 'there is no X the member did not borrow' — the double-NOT-EXISTS division pattern (or NOT EXISTS over EXCEPT).

items.q: **(Silberschatz, Ex. 3.21d)** To find the average books borrowed per member, counting members who borrowed nothing as 0, you must:
options: Use an outer join so members absent from 'borrowed' still count, or divide total borrows by total members
items.explain: An inner join silently drops members with no borrowings, biasing the average upward. An outer join (or total-borrows ÷ total-members) includes the zero-borrowers correctly.

items.q: **(Silberschatz, Ex. 3.23)** A query uses `WITH dept_total AS (...), dept_total_avg AS (...)`. The exercise asks to rewrite it WITHOUT the with construct, by:
options: Replacing each CTE with an equivalent subquery in the FROM clause
items.explain: A non-recursive CTE is syntactic sugar for a derived table; each WITH block can be inlined as a subquery in FROM (with an alias).

items.q: **(Silberschatz, Ex. 3.30)** `SELECT avg(salary) - (sum(salary)/count(*)) FROM instructor` is not always 0. Why?
options: When some salary is NULL: avg and sum ignore the nulls, but count(*) counts those rows too
items.explain: avg(salary) and sum(salary) skip NULL salaries, but count(*) counts all rows including the null ones — so sum/count(*) divides by a larger denominator and differs from avg.

items.q: **(Silberschatz, Practice Ex. 4.1)** `instructor NATURAL JOIN teaches NATURAL JOIN section NATURAL JOIN course` returns too few rows. What is wrong?
options: instructor and course both have dept_name, so the natural join wrongly also equates dept_name, dropping valid rows
items.explain: Natural join equates ALL same-named columns. Since both instructor and course carry dept_name, it adds an unintended equality and removes rows where they differ. Use JOIN ... USING to control the columns.

items.q: **(Silberschatz, Ex. 4.16)** 'Find each student who has NEVER taken a course', using no subqueries or set operations, is done with:
options: A LEFT OUTER JOIN of student to takes, keeping rows where the takes columns are NULL
items.explain: student LEFT OUTER JOIN takes ... WHERE takes.ID IS NULL — the unmatched (NULL-padded) rows are exactly the students with no enrolment. This is the anti-join idiom.

items.q: **(Silberschatz, Practice Ex. 4.3)** The exercise shows outer joins can be computed without the outer-join operator. A LEFT OUTER JOIN equals:
options: The inner join UNION the unmatched left rows padded with NULLs
items.explain: A left outer join = (inner join result) ∪ (left rows with no match, extended with nulls). This decomposition is what the exercise asks you to write explicitly.

items.q: **(Silberschatz, Practice Ex. 4.11)** Why do database systems offer many kinds of authorization, when operating systems usually offer only read and write on files?
options: Because a DBMS must control access at the granularity of operations (select/insert/update/delete) on specific tables, columns, and views
They do not — DBs also offer only two
items.explain: A database needs finer control than a file system: distinct privileges per operation and per object (table/column/view), plus the ability to grant on derived data.

items.q: **(Silberschatz, Practice Ex. 4.13)** If a user is granted only SELECT on a view v (defined over relation r), do they need SELECT on r as well?
options: No — authorization on the view is sufficient; they need not have access to the base relation r
Only if r has a primary key
items.explain: A view can grant access to derived data without exposing the base table — a core security use of views. The user queries v without any privilege on r.

items.q: **(Silberschatz, Ex. 4.26)** What is the difference between integrity constraints and authorization constraints?
options: Integrity constraints restrict the data values allowed; authorization constraints restrict which users may perform which operations
items.explain: Integrity constraints (keys, checks, referential rules) govern valid data states; authorization constraints (grants/roles) govern who is permitted to access or modify data.

items.q: **(Silberschatz §5.2)** In `create procedure dept_count_proc(in dept_name varchar(20), out d_count integer)`, the in and out keywords indicate:
options: in = a parameter given a value by the caller; out = a parameter whose value is set in the procedure to return a result
items.explain: IN parameters are supplied by the caller; OUT parameters are assigned inside the procedure and returned. The procedure is invoked with the call statement.

items.q: **(Silberschatz §5.3, Fig. 5.10)** In trigger `credits_earned AFTER UPDATE OF grade ON takes ... referencing new row as nrow`, what does `for each row` ensure?
options: The trigger runs once per SQL statement
The trigger body executes once for each row affected by the update
Only the first row is processed
items.explain: FOR EACH ROW makes it a row-level trigger: an UPDATE touching many rows fires the body for each one, using nrow/orow (transition variables) for the new/old values.

items.q: **(Elmasri/Navathe, Review 7.2)** What is the conceptual order in which the clauses of an SQL retrieval query are executed?
options: SELECT, FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, ORDER BY
FROM, WHERE, GROUP BY, HAVING, SELECT, ORDER BY
WHERE, GROUP BY, FROM, SELECT, ORDER BY, HAVING
FROM, SELECT, WHERE, HAVING, GROUP BY, ORDER BY
items.explain: Conceptually: FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY. This ordering explains NULL/aggregate behaviour and alias visibility.

items.q: **(Elmasri/Navathe, Review 7.3)** How are NULLs treated by aggregate functions and in grouping?
options: Aggregates count NULLs; grouping ignores them
Aggregates (except COUNT(*)) ignore NULLs; in grouping, all NULLs form a single group
NULLs cause aggregates to return NULL always
items.explain: Aggregates skip NULLs (COUNT(*) excepted). For GROUP BY, the rows with NULL in the grouping attribute are gathered into one group (NULLs treated as equal).

items.q: **(Elmasri/Navathe, Review 7.4e)** How does an assertion differ from a trigger?
options: An assertion is a passive constraint that must always remain true; a trigger is an active rule that performs an action when an event occurs
An assertion runs code; a trigger checks a condition
items.explain: An assertion declaratively forbids any database state violating a condition; a trigger is procedural (event-condition-action), firing an action on inserts/updates/deletes.

items.q: **(Elmasri/Navathe, Ex. 7.5a)** 'For each department whose AVERAGE salary exceeds $30,000, retrieve the department name and number of employees' requires:
options: GROUP BY Dno with HAVING AVG(Salary) > 30000, selecting COUNT(*)
items.explain: Group employees by department, filter groups with HAVING AVG(Salary) > 30000 (an aggregate condition belongs in HAVING, not WHERE), and report COUNT(*) per surviving group.

items.q: **(Elmasri/Navathe, Ex. 7.6a)** 'Retrieve names of straight-A students (grade A in ALL their courses)' is a division query. Contrast it with Ex. 7.6b 'students who do NOT have an A in ANY course':
options: 7.6a needs double NOT EXISTS (no course without an A); 7.6b needs a single NOT EXISTS (no course with an A)
items.explain: 'A in ALL courses' is universal quantification → double NOT EXISTS. 'Not an A in ANY course' is a single negated existential → one NOT EXISTS. 'All' ⇒ two negations; 'any' ⇒ one.

items.q: **(Elmasri/Navathe, Ex. 7.7a)** 'Retrieve names of employees who work in the department that has the employee with the highest salary in the whole company' is naturally written with:
options: Nested subqueries — find the max-salary employee's Dno via a subquery, then select employees of that department
items.explain: Use nesting: an inner subquery locates the department of the company-wide highest earner (e.g. Dno of the employee whose Salary = MAX), and the outer query lists that department's employees.

items.q: **(Elmasri/Navathe, Ex. 7.9)** On `DEPT_SUMMARY(D, C, Total_s, Average_s)` defined with GROUP BY Dno and aggregates COUNT/SUM/AVG, which operations are allowed?
options: SELECT queries on the view are allowed, but UPDATE/DELETE are not (it is a non-updatable, aggregated view)
items.explain: Because the view uses GROUP BY and aggregate functions, each view row summarises many base rows and cannot be mapped back to one — so it is read-only: queries work, modifications are rejected.
